title: Will for Decisions, Offers and Promises
summary: Use will to announce a decision made while speaking, offer or agree to help, make a promise, and recognise refusal with won’t. Use Shall I…? for offers and Shall we…? for shared suggestions, while Will you…? normally asks someone else to do something.
learningObjectives: Choose will or the contraction ’ll to announce a spontaneous decision rather than describe an existing arrangement.
Offer help, accept a request and make a specific promise using will or won’t.
Interpret won’t as refusal or unwillingness, including when equipment fails to work.
Form Shall I…? and Shall we…? questions and distinguish them from requests beginning Will you…?

explanation.heading: Decisions made as you speak
explanation.body: Use will + the base form when a choice is made at the moment it is announced. A new problem, question or offer can trigger the decision. In informal conversation, I will usually becomes I’ll. With I think and I don’t think, will also makes a decision sound less abrupt. Do not use a plain present-simple statement to announce this new choice.
explanation.example: I forgot to bring a pen. I’ll borrow one from reception.

explanation.heading: Offers and agreeing to requests
explanation.body: Use I’ll when you volunteer to do something, and when you agree to a request. An offer is the speaker’s own action, while a request asks the listener to act. Give the action after will in its base form: I’ll carry, not I’ll carrying.
explanation.example: Those folders look awkward. I’ll hold the door for you.

explanation.heading: Promises and reassurance
explanation.body: Use will to commit to future action and won’t to promise not to do something. I promise can make the commitment explicit, but it is not required. A reply such as I won’t forget gives reassurance about the speaker’s future behaviour. Will not is often shortened to won’t, not willn’t.
explanation.example: I’ll send the notes tonight, and I won’t share your password.

explanation.heading: Refusal and unwillingness with won’t
explanation.body: Won’t can describe someone’s refusal to cooperate rather than a simple future negative. The same form can describe a device that fails to respond despite repeated attempts; the device is not literally making a choice. Use context to decide whether won’t reports refusal, failed operation or a promise.
explanation.example: I’ve pressed the button twice, but the printer won’t start.

explanation.heading: Shall I, shall we and will you
explanation.body: Use Shall I…? to ask whether you should do something for someone; use Shall we…? to suggest an action together. What shall I/we…? asks for advice or a joint decision. Will you…? normally asks the listener to act, and please can soften the request. Shall in these questions is particularly associated with British English; would you and should I may be more familiar elsewhere.
explanation.example: Shall I move the chairs, or shall we leave them here?

comparisons.title: A new decision versus a prior arrangement

left.label: Will: decided just now
left.example: The charger is missing. I’ll ask the office for a spare.
left.note: The problem leads to a decision at the moment of speaking.

right.label: Present continuous: arranged earlier
right.example: I’m collecting my repaired laptop at four.
right.note: The collection was organised before the speaker said this.

comparisons.title: Offer to act versus request to another person

left.label: Shall I…?: I act
left.example: Shall I carry this box upstairs?
left.note: The speaker asks permission to help.

right.label: Will you…?: you act
right.example: Will you carry this box upstairs, please?
right.note: The speaker requests an action from the listener.

examples.sentence: There is no clean cup. I’ll rinse this one.
examples.note: The speaker chooses an immediate solution.

examples.sentence: I think I’ll take a short break before the next meeting.
examples.note: I think makes a just-made choice more tentative.

examples.sentence: Yes, I’ll give Nia the message as soon as she gets back.
examples.note: The speaker agrees to carry out a request.

examples.sentence: Don’t worry, I won’t post that photo online.
examples.note: Won’t expresses a promise not to act.

examples.sentence: Shall we compare the two designs before making a choice?
examples.note: Shall we proposes a shared action rather than predicting the future.

commonMistakes.incorrect: I forgot the attachment. I send it now.
commonMistakes.correct: I forgot the attachment. I’ll send it now.
commonMistakes.why: A decision made on discovering the mistake is naturally announced with I’ll, not the present simple.

commonMistakes.incorrect: I’ll helping you move the desk.
commonMistakes.correct: I’ll help you move the desk.
commonMistakes.why: Will is followed by the base verb help, not the -ing form.
Won’t is the standard negative contraction of will not.

commonMistakes.incorrect: Shall you turn the light off, please?
commonMistakes.correct: Will you turn the light off, please?
commonMistakes.why: Use Will you…? to request that the listener act; Shall I…? offers the speaker’s action.

studyTips: Before choosing will for an action, ask whether the decision was made only after the current conversation began.
Practise a three-part exchange: hear a problem, offer help with I’ll, then respond to a request with I’ll or won’t.
Make paired questions using the same verb: Shall I open…? and Will you open…? Notice who is expected to act.

exercises.prompt: You have just noticed that the kitchen light is still on. You decide this instant to switch it off. “Oh, ___ it off now.”
choices: I switch
I’ll switch
I’m switching yesterday
exercises.feedback: I’ll switch announces a decision made as the speaker notices the light.

exercises.prompt: Your coworker is carrying several boxes. You volunteer to help. Which response is most natural?
choices: I’ll carry one for you.
Shall you carry one for me?
I carrying one for you.
exercises.feedback: I’ll carry one for you offers to perform an action for the coworker.

exercises.prompt: Someone asks you to keep a surprise confidential. Choose the promise.
choices: I won’t telling anyone.
I don’t think I tell anyone.
I won’t tell anyone.
exercises.feedback: Won’t plus the base form tell is a natural negative promise.

exercises.prompt: You would like your colleague to lower the blinds. Which question asks THEM to do it?
choices: Shall I lower the blinds?
Will you lower the blinds, please?
Shall we lower the blinds together?
exercises.feedback: Will you…? requests action from the listener, whereas Shall I…? offers your own action.

exercises.prompt: You have just noticed a spelling mistake. “___ it right away.” (begin with I; use the contracted form of will and correct)
acceptedAnswers: I'll correct
exercises.feedback: I’ll correct announces the new decision to fix the mistake immediately.

exercises.prompt: A friend asks, “Can you bring the spare key?” Reply: “Sure, I ___ it.” (bring; use the full form will)
acceptedAnswers: will bring
exercises.feedback: Will bring agrees to carry out the request, with bring in its base form.

exercises.prompt: Your phone refuses to charge even with a working cable. “My phone ___.” (charge; use the negative contraction of will)
acceptedAnswers: won't charge
exercises.feedback: Won’t charge can describe a device that fails to operate despite attempts.

exercises.prompt: You and your classmate need to choose a topic together. “___ we choose the first topic?” (use the suggestion word from this unit)
acceptedAnswers: Shall
exercises.feedback: Shall we…? makes a suggestion about a shared action.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence. The speaker has just made a decision: I check the delivery address now.
acceptedAnswers: I’ll check the delivery address now.
I will check the delivery address now.
exercises.feedback: When the decision is made while speaking, will or I’ll naturally announces it.

exercises.prompt: Correct the verb form in this offer: I will carrying your suitcase upstairs.
acceptedAnswers: I will carry your suitcase upstairs.
I'll carry your suitcase upstairs.
exercises.feedback: The base verb carry must follow will; carrying is not grammatical here.

exercises.prompt: Correct the negative contraction in this promise: I willn’t use your account without asking.
acceptedAnswers: I won’t use your account without asking.
I will not use your account without asking.
exercises.feedback: Won’t, not willn’t, is the contraction of will not.

exercises.prompt: Correct the first word in this question. You are asking the other person to turn down the sound: Shall you turn down the sound, please?
acceptedAnswers: Will you turn down the sound, please?
exercises.feedback: Will you…? asks another person to act; Shall I…? would offer to do it yourself.

speakingExercises.prompt: The parcel has arrived unexpectedly. Decide now to open it. Say one sentence starting “I” and ending “the parcel now”. Use will and the verb open.
acceptedAnswers: I'll open the parcel now.
I will open the parcel now.
speakingExercises.feedback: Will announces the decision made at this moment, followed by open in the base form.

speakingExercises.prompt: A friend has two heavy bags. Offer to carry one for them. Begin with “I” and use will, carry, one bag and for you.
acceptedAnswers: I'll carry one bag for you.
I will carry one bag for you.
speakingExercises.feedback: I’ll carry makes a practical offer; one bag keeps the response specific.

speakingExercises.prompt: A colleague asks, “Can you email me the minutes?” Agree in a single sentence beginning “Yes,” and say that you will send them the minutes tonight.
acceptedAnswers: Yes, I'll send you the minutes tonight.
Yes, I will send you the minutes tonight.
speakingExercises.feedback: The speaker agrees to perform the requested action. Will is followed by send.

speakingExercises.prompt: You promise not to tell anyone about a surprise. Say one sentence beginning “I” using the negative of will and the verb tell.
acceptedAnswers: I won't tell anyone about the surprise.
I will not tell anyone about the surprise.
speakingExercises.feedback: Won’t tell is a commitment to keep the surprise secret.

speakingExercises.prompt: Ask whether you should open the door for the listener. Begin “Shall I” and end “the door?”
acceptedAnswers: Shall I open the door?
speakingExercises.feedback: Shall I…? asks whether the speaker should perform the action.

speakingExercises.prompt: You and a friend are deciding what to do together. Suggest checking the timetable. Begin “Shall we”.
acceptedAnswers: Shall we check the timetable?
speakingExercises.feedback: Shall we…? offers a suggestion for both people.

speakingExercises.prompt: A radio is too loud. Ask the listener to make it quieter. Begin “Will you” and use “turn the radio down” plus “please”.
acceptedAnswers: Will you turn the radio down, please?
Will you please turn the radio down?
speakingExercises.feedback: Will you…? asks the listener to act. The position of please can vary.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say exactly two sentences: first state that the scanner refuses to work, beginning “The scanner”; then offer to call technical support, beginning “I” and using will.
acceptedAnswers: The scanner won't work. I'll call technical support.
The scanner will not work. I'll call technical support.
The scanner won't work. I will call technical support.
The scanner will not work. I will call technical support.
speakingExercises.feedback: Won’t work reports failed operation; I’ll call offers an immediate response.

listeningExercises.audioText: The lift is broken again. Oh well, I’ll take the stairs to the fourth floor.
listeningExercises.prompt: Why does the speaker say they will use the stairs?
choices: They agreed yesterday to use them.
They decide on the spot because the lift is broken.
They have already taken the stairs.
listeningExercises.feedback: The broken lift creates a new situation and I’ll take announces an immediate decision.

listeningExercises.audioText: You have a large suitcase. Wait a moment and I’ll hold the door for you.
listeningExercises.prompt: What is the speaker offering to do?
choices: Hold the door for someone.
Ask the other person to hold the door.
Close the door after everyone leaves.
listeningExercises.feedback: I’ll hold the door is an offer by the speaker, not a request addressed to the listener.

listeningExercises.audioText: You can trust me. I won't reveal your secret to anyone at work.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the two-word promise immediately after “I” and before “your secret”.
acceptedAnswers: won't reveal
will not reveal
listeningExercises.feedback: The heard phrase is won’t reveal; will not reveal is an accepted full-form equivalent.

listeningExercises.audioText: This box is heavier than I expected. Will you help me carry it upstairs, please?
listeningExercises.prompt: What is the speaker asking the other person to do?
choices: Help the speaker carry a box.
Suggest a different box.
Let the speaker carry the box alone.
listeningExercises.feedback: Will you help me…? is a polite request for the listener to help.

listeningExercises.audioText: We have two possible routes to the station. Shall we compare their travel times first?
choices: The speaker should choose the first route alone.
Both people should compare the routes.
The listener must use the shorter route.
listeningExercises.feedback: Shall we compare…? proposes an action the two people can take together.

listeningExercises.audioText: I charged this tablet overnight, but it still won’t turn on this morning.
listeningExercises.prompt: What problem is the speaker describing?
choices: Someone will not answer a message.
The tablet has already been repaired.
A tablet is failing to turn on.
listeningExercises.feedback: Won’t turn on describes equipment that refuses to operate despite attempts.

listeningExercises.audioText: I can see the instructions are confusing. I'll help you with the form.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the two-word offer heard immediately before “you with the form”.
acceptedAnswers: I'll help
listeningExercises.feedback: The speaker offers to help; the two audible words are I’ll help.

listeningExercises.audioText: There is nowhere for our guest to sit. Shall I bring another chair?
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the single word immediately before “I bring another chair?”
acceptedAnswers: Shall
listeningExercises.feedback: The word Shall begins Shall I…?, which asks if the listener would like the speaker to act.
